title: Why melting ice stays at 0 °C
body: In ice, water particles are locked in a regular pattern and can only jiggle in place. In liquid water they still touch, but they slide past each other in a jumble.

Heating usually makes particles move faster, and that's what a thermometer measures. While ice melts, though, the energy goes into breaking particles free of the pattern instead. They don't speed up, so the temperature stays at 0 °C until all the ice has gone.

That hidden energy is called the latent heat of fusion. Melting 1 g of ice takes about 334 J, enough to warm 1 g of liquid water by about 80 °C. A stronger heater melts the ice sooner, but the mix still sits at 0 °C while it melts.
equation: Energy to melt = mass × 334 J/g (for ice)
realWorld: Ice keeps a drink near 0 °C until it has all melted, which is why a cool box full of ice works so well. Boiling water does the same at 100 °C: turning the stove up makes it boil faster, not hotter.
